summary: LUNA NAVIGATOR is an intelligent lunar mission-planning platform designed to answer one critical question: Where and when can we land on the Moon safely while maintaining power and communication? We developed an interactive web-based solution that transforms NASA lunar terrain data and JPL celestial-position information into actionable landing-site intelligence. Using NASA's LOLA 80 m/pixel Digital Elevation Model and NASA/JPL Horizons data, it analyses terrain elevation, surface slopes, local horizons, sunlight availability, and direct-to-Earth communication visibility. It combines these factors through multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), enabling users to compare candidate landing locations, evaluate mission timelines, examine power and communication windows, and identify more suitable landing opportunities.Unlike systems that consider terrain safety or illumination in isolation, LUNA NAVIGATOR brings terrain, power sustainability, and communication reliability into one unified decision-support platform. Its interactive visualisation and scenario-comparison capabilities make complex lunar environmental data easier to interpret.This project addresses a major challenge in lunar exploration: selecting landing locations that are not only physically suitable but also operationally sustainable. By helping mission planners identify potential risks and evaluate trade-offs before landing, LUNA NAVIGATOR supports safer, better-informed, and more efficient future lunar missions.
details:
Project Overview

LUNA NAVIGATOR is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to identify and evaluate suitable landing locations on the Moon, particularly in the lunar south-polar region. It addresses three critical mission requirements: terrain safety, sustainable power availability, and reliable communication with Earth.

Working Principle and Methodology

The platform uses NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) Digital Elevation Model (DEM), specifically the 80 m/pixel south-polar elevation dataset, to analyse lunar surface elevation, terrain slope, and local horizon profiles. It also integrates NASA/JPL Horizons data to obtain celestial-position information for the Sun and Earth.

The system processes these datasets to estimate sunlight availability, solar power opportunities, direct-to-Earth communication visibility, and potential communication blackout periods. It combines these parameters using Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) to compare candidate landing sites and support informed mission-planning decisions.

Users can explore locations, compare scenarios, evaluate mission timelines, and examine the trade-offs between different landing options through an interactive interface.

Key Benefits and Features

Improved Landing-Site Assessment: Evaluates terrain elevation and slope to help identify potentially hazardous areas.

Power Planning: Analyses sunlight availability to understand opportunities for solar energy generation.

Communication Planning: Estimates direct-to-Earth visibility and potential communication interruptions.

Comparative Analysis: Allows multiple candidate landing sites and mission scenarios to be evaluated using consistent criteria.

Data-Driven Decisions: Converts complex lunar datasets into understandable visualisations and comparative assessments.

Reduced Planning Uncertainty: Helps identify operational constraints before a mission is carried out.

Intended Impact

LUNA NAVIGATOR aims to support safer, more reliable, and more sustainable lunar exploration. By bringing terrain, illumination, and communication analysis into one platform, it helps mission planners understand environmental conditions that may affect lunar landing and subsequent surface operations.

The project is particularly relevant to future lunar south-pole missions, where terrain conditions, permanently shadowed regions, changing illumination, and communication constraints make landing-site selection challenging. It can serve as a decision-support foundation for future lunar exploration research and mission planning.

Technologies and Tools Used

Programming Languages and Frameworks

Python – Data processing, scientific calculations, and backend logic.

FastAPI – Backend API development.

JavaScript – Frontend application development.

React and Vite – Interactive user interface.

Visualisation and Data Technologies:

Three.js and Cesium – Interactive lunar visualisation.

NASA LOLA DEM – Lunar elevation and terrain data.

NASA/JPL Horizons API – Sun and Earth ephemeris information.

NumPy and scientific Python tools – Numerical and geospatial computations.

Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) – Comparative evaluation and ranking of candidate sites.

Development and Deployment Tools

Visual Studio Code – Development environment.

Git and GitHub – Version control and source-code management.

Docker – Local containerised development.

Vercel – Frontend deployment.

Render – Backend deployment.

The project was developed and tested using a computer with internet connectivity; no specialised physical hardware was required.

Creativity and Innovation

The key innovation of LUNA NAVIGATOR is that it does not evaluate lunar landing locations using only one parameter. Instead, it combines terrain characteristics, solar illumination, and Earth communication visibility into a unified mission-planning workflow.

It uses real NASA lunar elevation data rather than relying entirely on artificially generated terrain. Its terrain-aware horizon analysis considers surrounding surface geometry when evaluating celestial visibility. The platform also combines scientific calculations with interactive visualisation, scenario comparison, and multi-criteria evaluation.

This integration makes complex lunar environmental information more accessible and useful for comparing potential mission locations.

Key Factors Considered

Terrain Safety: Elevation variations, surface slopes, and surrounding terrain obstructions.

Solar Illumination: Sun visibility, illumination duration, and potential solar power availability.

Communication Reliability: Earth visibility, communication opportunities, and possible blackout periods.

Geographical Accuracy: Use of NASA LOLA elevation data and appropriate lunar coordinate handling.

Time-Dependent Conditions: Changes in the positions of the Sun and Earth over a mission timeline.

Decision-Making: Combining multiple mission requirements instead of prioritising only one factor.

Usability: Presenting complex scientific results through an interactive and understandable interface.

Scalability: Designing the system so that additional landing sites, datasets, and mission-planning capabilities can be incorporated.

Conclusion

LUNA NAVIGATOR transforms lunar terrain and environmental data into meaningful mission-planning intelligence, helping future lunar exploration move towards safer landings and more sustainable surface operations.
